country.comment: Study conducted in the Santa Rosa neighborhood of Guarujá City, São Paulo State, Brazil.

effect_estimate.comment: No regression models, 95% confidence intervals, or p-values are reported; empirical findings are descriptive percentages across SDI-stratified groups and municipal SNIS/Census comparisons.
effect_estimate.value: Descriptive percentages only (no inferential regression estimates, CIs, or p-values reported): across N = 393 surveyed households in 7 SDI-defined groups, water supply provision ranged from 98.48% (Group 5) to 100.00% (Groups 1-4, 6-7) with 72.58% to 83.08% rating water supply as adequate, whereas sanitation (sewage) provision varied from 68.18% (Group 5) and 76.47% (Group 4) to 100.00% (Groups 3 and 7) with only 27.27% to 50.79% rating sanitation as adequate (Table 4; text/Figure 3 also report non-provision of sanitation at 29.2% in Group 1, 15.2% in Group 5, and 11.8% in Group 4). Regarding planning and participation mechanisms, most interviewees reported never having knowledge of or access to the municipal basic sanitation and solid waste plans (exact percentage not reported), although a significant portion considered access important. Following Guarujá's 2010 Municipal Basic Sanitation Plan (which legally barred supplying irregular areas) and its revision under Complementary Law 228/2018 (incorporating irregular areas into planned expansion), municipal SNIS sewage coverage rose by 6.33 percentage points since 2010 to 70.05% in 2020, while water supply coverage fell by 3.82 percentage points from 86.39% in 2010 to 82.57% in 2020.
effect_estimate.where_found: PDF pp. 13-14, Figure 3; PDF pp. 18-20, Table 4 and Results and discussion

mechanism_certainty.comment: Rated 1 (within the maximum ceiling of 2 for a cross-sectional JBI study): the study empirically documents descriptive disparities in water/sanitation coverage and perceived adequacy across SDI groups alongside residents' reported lack of access to municipal sanitation plans, and cites statutory changes from the 2010 plan's legal prohibition on serving irregular areas to Complementary Law 228/2018's inclusion of irregular areas, but the causal operation of legal/planning mechanisms on household access is posited descriptively rather than directly observed or quasi-experimentally tested.
mechanism_certainty.where_found: PDF p. 14; PDF pp. 18-20, Table 4 and Results and discussion

mechanism_flags.comment: Examines municipal basic sanitation and master planning legislation (Complementary Laws 108/2007, 227/2018, and 228/2018; Law 11,445/2007), prior legal restrictions prohibiting sanitation provision in irregular settlement areas versus planned service-area expansion to irregular areas under Complementary Law 228/2018, and public access/social participation in municipal plans (Questions 8-9).

sample_size.comment: Minimum simple random sample estimated at 390 households (12% acceptable sampling error); 393 household questionnaires were applied across 7 SDI-stratified groups (65, 63, 62, 68, 66, 60, and 9 questionnaires in Groups 1-7, respectively) covering 6,573 private households in 32 census sectors of the Santa Rosa neighborhood.
sample_size.value: 393 households (questionnaires applied across 7 SDI-defined groups out of 6,573 private households in 32 census sectors)
sample_size.where_found: PDF pp. 9-10, Methodology and Table 2; PDF p. 11, Results and discussion

study_design.comment: Structured 9-question closed-ended household survey applied across 7 census-sector block groupings stratified via the Social Development Index (SDI), analysed quantitatively as percentages, mapped in ArcGIS, and compared descriptively with 2010 IBGE Census/SNIS data and municipal sanitation laws/plans.
study_design.value: Cross-sectional stratified household questionnaire survey with GIS spatialization and descriptive comparison with census data and municipal sanitation plans
study_design.where_found: PDF p. 1, Abstract; PDF pp. 8-10, Methodology; PDF p. 30, Appendix I
